<explanation>
Based on our analysis of the file tree and README, we can see that Monifactory is a complex Minecraft modpack that “remasters” and ports a previous modpack (Nomifactory CEu) and integrates many mods like GregTech CEu Modern along with several additional modifications. This project is therefore a modpack with a heavy focus on custom configuration overrides, KubeJS scripting for in-game logic modifications, and integration with multiple external mods. When drawing your system design diagram, you should capture as many discrete components and interactions as possible. Here’s how to proceed:

1. Identify the main components:
   • Core Modpack Assets & Configuration – these include the “config”, “config-overrides” (with separate directories for normal, hardmode, and expert), defaultconfigs files, and override files. These components illustrate the modpack’s mechanism for supporting multiple progression modes.
   • KubeJS Engine – The “kubejs” directory is the backbone for custom client and server scripts. It contains subdirectories for client_scripts, server_scripts, startup_scripts, data, assets, and even tooling (like dx, eslint config, package.json). These scripts control recipe changes, mod tweaks, and integration logic.
   • Build & Packaging Tools – The “tools” directory (with its bootstrap and build subfolders) and the pack-mode-switcher scripts (pack-mode-switcher.bat and .sh) are responsible for packaging, building, and switching among game modes. They automate tasks such as modifying recipes and generating configuration files.
   • Mod Integration & Compatibility – The “mods” folder and the instructions for addon mods (Create, XNet, etc.) indicate that the pack is designed to work with various external mods. Depict these as external dependencies interfacing with the core modpack.
   • CI/CD and Repository-Oriented Components – The presence of the .github folder (with issue templates, workflows, GitHub Actions for builds and linting) indicates automated tests and build pipelines.

2. Show relationships and interactions:
   • Draw a central “Modpack Runtime” block representing Minecraft as modified by the modpack. From that, show arrows toward this runtime from:
       – “Config / Overrides” (which supply game settings, difficulty modes, and mod configurations)
       – “KubeJS Scripts” (both client-side and server-side modifications that alter in-game behavior and recipes)
       – “External Mods & Optional Compat Modules” (whose integration points are handled by KubeJS scripts and override configurations)
   • Include the “Build & Packaging Pipeline” which is responsible for assembling the modpack – from “tools” (build scripts and code generation) and the “pack-mode-switcher” that selects the correct mode based on user input. Illustrate that these tools feed the “Config / Overrides”.
   • Indicate the CI/CD process (GitHub workflows) as a supporting subsystem that automatically runs linting, tests, and builds whenever changes are pushed.

3. Highlight important architectural patterns and design principles:
   • Modularity and Mode Switching – The separation of config overrides into “normal”, “hardmode”, and “expert” shows an architectural decision to support multiple difficulty/progression modes. Represent these as independent modules that merge into the overall configuration.
   • Script-Driven Behavior Modification – KubeJS scripts (divided into startup, client, server, and fixes) are the “glue” between base mod functionality and the custom progression logic. Make sure to denote the “data flow” (arrows) that indicate their hook into the mod processing pipeline.
   • Automated Build/Deployment – The integration of GitHub Actions, tools for code generation (including credits and language files), and pack-mode switcher utilities depicts a robust development and deployment pipeline.

4. Include relevant technologies and libraries:
   • KubeJS (for in-game scripting)
   • JavaScript (node.js used in the “tools” directory and within KubeJS scripts)
   • Minecraft Forge server (for the dedicated server setup instructions)
   • GitHub Actions for CI/CD
   • Various configuration formats (JSON, TOML, YAML, SNBT) are used for mod configurations. Represent these file types as part of your “Configuration Store.”

5. Tailor the diagram to this modpack-style project:
   • For a Minecraft modpack like this, emphasize the separation between the build/configuration pipeline (pack-mode switching and build tools), the core configuration and mod integration (config-overrides and defaultconfigs), and the custom behavior implemented via KubeJS.
   • On your diagram, clearly label each module (e.g., “Core Config,” “KubeJS – Client Scripts,” “KubeJS – Server Scripts,” “Pack-Mode Switcher,” “External Mod Dependencies,” “CI/CD Pipeline”) and use directional arrows to show dependency flows (for instance, build scripts generate/configure overrides, which then get picked up by the game engine at runtime after KubeJS has modified recipe/data flows).

6. Guidelines for the diagram’s visual elements:
   • Use distinct shapes or colors to represent different categories. For example:
       – Rectangles for core components (Config, KubeJS, Tools, Mods)
       – Rounded shapes for external systems (CI/CD, external mod dependencies)
       – Arrows with clear labels (e.g., “configuration override”, “runtime hook”, “build pipeline”)
   • Include annotations where appropriate, such as notes on “Mode Switching” (highlighting forced Peaceful mode and difficulty-specific overrides) and “Script Execution Order” (startup > client/server scripts > fixes).
   • Ensure that your diagram’s layout is logical (perhaps a layered architecture starting with build/config on top, core runtime in the center, and external systems at the periphery).

In summary, your system design diagram should visually capture the modular and layered architecture of Monifactory – showcasing the build process, mode-based configuration overrides, the central KubeJS-driven transformation of mod behavior, and how all these pieces interact with the Minecraft runtime environment as well as with externally integrated mods. This highly detailed, “component-by-component” representation will serve as an excellent communication tool for understanding and further developing the system’s architecture.
</explanation>
